brief.topic: The People Hidden in Two Overlapping Lists

s01: Two lists can contain fewer people than their lengths suggest.
Six people joined the drawing workshop. Five joined the music workshop.
Three people joined both. How many different people joined at least one?
Put the two lists side by side. Adding their lengths gives eleven entries.
But these three names appear twice.
Pair each repeated name with its other copy.
Keep one copy of each person and remove the duplicates.
Eight different people remain.
That is six plus five, minus three.
The subtraction does not remove people who enjoy both workshops.
It removes their extra count. They still belong in our answer.
This is the two-set inclusion and exclusion rule.
Count the first group, add the second, then subtract their overlap once.
Someone in one group is counted once. Someone in both is counted twice and corrected back to once.
Now imagine one more person joins the music workshop.
If that person is already on the drawing list, how does the total change?
The music count grows by one, but the overlap also grows by one. The total stays eight.
If instead a completely new person joins, the overlap stays three.
Then the total becomes nine.
Before adding two counts, ask whether they count some of the same things.

scenes.narration:
Two lists can contain fewer people than their lengths suggest. Six people joined the drawing workshop. Five joined the music workshop. Three people joined both. How many different people joined at least one?

Put the two lists side by side. Adding their lengths gives eleven entries. But these three names appear twice. Pair each repeated name with its other copy. Keep one copy of each person and remove the duplicates. Eight different people remain.

That is six plus five, minus three. The subtraction does not remove people who enjoy both workshops. It removes their extra count. They still belong in our answer.

This is the two-set inclusion and exclusion rule. Count the first group, add the second, then subtract their overlap once. Someone in one group is counted once. Someone in both is counted twice and corrected back to once.

Now imagine one more person joins the music workshop. If that person is already on the drawing list, how does the total change? The music count grows by one, but the overlap also grows by one. The total stays eight.

If instead a completely new person joins, the overlap stays three. Then the total becomes nine. Before adding two counts, ask whether they count some of the same things.
